title: Mamata Banerjee Calls Delimitation BJP's Tool to Divide Bengal and India
excerpt: West Bengal CM attacks Centre's plan to expand Lok Sabha to 850 seats, warns NRC and detention camps will follow
body:
• West Bengal CM Mamata Banerjee has accused the BJP of using the Delimitation Bill to divide Bengal and India, calling it a move made "for political mileage"
  • The Union Government introduced three bills that could expand the Lok Sabha from 545 to up to 850 seats, based on the 2011 Census
  • Banerjee warned that delimitation would be followed by the National Register of Citizens (NRC), leading to mass voter deletions and detention camps
  • She alleged the BJP plans to trifurcate West Bengal, potentially merging districts with Bihar and Odisha

West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee has launched a sharp attack on the BJP-led central government over the proposed Delimitation Bill, calling it a deliberate tool to fracture West Bengal and the country at large.

Speaking at election rallies across the state, the Trinamool Congress supremo said the BJP was pushing the legislation "for political mileage at a time when they don't have a majority," noting the ruling party depends on the support of two coalition partners to stay in power.

What the Bills Propose

The Union Government has circulated three bills that would pave the way for fresh delimitation based on the latest notified Census. The most consequential change: the strength of the Lok Sabha could increase from the current 545 to a potential 850 members. Seats in state and Union territory assemblies would also increase to accommodate 33 per cent reservation for women in Parliament and state legislatures.

"They are tabling the delimitation bill to divide West Bengal and India at large. They are doing it for political mileage at a time when they don't have a majority. They are in power owing to the support of two other parties."

— Mamata Banerjee, West Bengal Chief Minister

The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill proposes to operationalize the women's reservation law before the 2029 parliamentary elections through a delimitation exercise based on the 2011 Census. Companion bills address implementation in the Union territories of Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir.

NRC and Voter Deletion Fears

Banerjee's sharpest criticism centered on what she sees as the bills' downstream consequences. She warned that delimitation would inevitably lead to the implementation of the National Register of Citizens (NRC) in West Bengal, resulting in mass voter deletions and the establishment of detention camps.

"The people of Bengal will be driven out, and you will bring people from outside and make them vote for you. Is that the plan?" she asked at a rally in Howrah. She cited the deletion of 91 lakh names during the state's Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, claiming that over 60 lakh Hindus and 30 lakh Muslims had been removed.

Banerjee pointed to the NRC exercise in Assam as a precedent, where lakhs of names were reportedly deleted, and warned a similar process could unfold in Bengal under a BJP government.

Trifurcation Allegations

The Trinamool Congress leader has also alleged that the BJP's delimitation plan aims to trifurcate West Bengal, potentially merging some districts with neighboring Bihar and Odisha. She argued this would change the state's demographic and geographical composition and subject Bengalis in those merged areas to "even more suffering."

"Using delimitation, they might merge some districts of Bengal with Bihar and Odisha. Our people will be put through even more suffering. Our government will not allow the formation of detention camps," she said during a rally in Bankura.

Political Context

Banerjee's offensive comes ahead of West Bengal Assembly elections. She has framed the delimitation debate as central to regional identity and autonomy, a message that resonates with her political base. The TMC leader also accused the BJP of using the women's reservation bill as a front for the delimitation exercise, arguing the real intention is to reshape political boundaries to the BJP's advantage.

The BJP has defended the bills as necessary for democratic representation and the implementation of women's reservation. The opposition Congress and several regional parties have expressed concerns about the census basis and the timing of the exercise, though positions vary across the political spectrum.

For NRIs with roots in West Bengal, the debate carries significant implications for home-state representation and the broader trajectory of Indian federalism.
